items.title: A mutation without an error path fails silently
items.body:
`apiRequest` does throw on the 422, with the server's readiness message, so the status mutation ends in its error state. The builder just never looks. The status mutation declares only `onSuccess`, and no JSX reads `statusMutation.error`. The form's red line shows `formError`, which only the save mutation's `onError` sets, and the line under the Trigger button reads the trigger mutation's error. So the operator clicks Move to ACTIVE, nothing visible happens, and the workflow stays a draft.

Give every mutation the same error surface: an `onError` that sets the shared message, or render `mutation.error` next to the control that started it.

- *The red line* is wired to save only.
- *Under Trigger* is wired to the trigger only.
- *Request failed.* is apiRequest's fallback, but nothing renders it here.

items.title: Copying query data into form state with an effect
items.body:
The builder keeps the form in local state and fills it from the workflow query in a `useEffect` that depends on `workflowQuery.data`. That effect runs every time the query's data object changes, not just on first load. React Query keeps the same object when a refetch returns identical data, but the pause changed the status, so the refetch triggered by the status mutation's invalidation produces a new object and the effect writes every saved value back into the form. The unsaved cron edit is overwritten, and so is any other unsaved change.

Common fixes: seed the form once per workflow id (or `key` the form component on it), or track a dirty flag and skip the sync while the form is dirty.

- Nothing keeps unsaved state apart or saves it with the status.

excerpts.quote: onSuccess: async () => { await queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["workflow", workflowId] });

items.title: Why another operator's workflow is a 404, not a 403
items.body:
`triggerWorkflowManually` first loads the workflow with the caller's visibility scope. For an operator the scope is "own", so the query only finds workflows they created; operator A's workflow is not found and the service throws **404 WORKFLOW_NOT_FOUND**. `assertCanManageWorkflow`, which would throw the 403 scope violation, comes after the load and is never reached here.

- *403 WORKFLOW_SCOPE_VIOLATION* needs the workflow to be visible first, and an operator never sees another operator's workflow.
- *201* is wrong: ownership is enforced through the scope.
- *409* is wrong: the status is never checked for an invisible workflow.

items.title: Why a missing value passes a less-than test
items.body:
`readPath` walks the dotted path through `{ payload, context }` and returns `null` as soon as a segment is missing. For `lt`, `compare` evaluates `Number(leftValue) < Number(rightValue)`. `Number(null)` is **0**, and 0 < 50 is true, so the rule matches and the step runs. The concepts doc gives the same trap with `gt -1`.

- *Every comparison false* is how NaN behaves; null is not NaN here.
- *NaN is never below 50* would be right for `undefined`, but `readPath` returns `null`.
- *Missing keys skip conditions* is wrong: the rule is evaluated normally on the null value.

excerpts.quote: and `Number(null)` is `0`, so `gt -1` matches a missing field

items.title: Why missed schedule ticks become a single run
items.body:
`dispatchScheduledRuns(now)` loads ACTIVE SCHEDULE workflows whose `nextScheduledAt` is at or before now. For each one it enqueues **one** run and then computes the next tick with `getNextScheduledAt(cron, now)`, starting from the current time rather than from the missed tick. After the outage the workflow gets one catch-up run, and its next time is the first tick after 03:30.

- *Three runs, one per interval* would need a loop over the missed ticks.
- *No run* is wrong: the overdue workflow is still due.
- *Three runs and 04:00* is wrong for the same reason as the first; the 04:00 part alone would be right for an hourly cron.

items.title: Why an analyst gets 403 even with a broken body
items.body:
`executeRoute` checks authorization before it touches the body. With a session actor present, it calls `assertPermission(actor, "workflow:write")`; the analyst row of the matrix has only `session:read` and `workflow:read`, so it throws **403 FORBIDDEN**. The body would be parsed on the next line, which is never reached. The request lifecycle doc explains why this order is right: it does not reveal schema details to callers who may not write.

- *500 from a ZodError* is what a writer with a bad body gets, not an analyst.
- *400 with field errors* is not produced anywhere in this code.
- *404* is wrong: analysts can see every workflow.

excerpts.quote: const body = options.bodySchema ? options.bodySchema.parse(await request.json()) : undefined;

items.title: Concept: three roles, two kinds of check
items.body:
Access is decided in two places, and they answer different questions.

**The permission matrix** in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` says what each role (ADMIN, OPERATOR, ANALYST) may do at all: read, write, publish, execute, ops. `executeRoute` in `src/lib/http/route-helpers.ts` applies a route's permission. Read `executeRoute` line by line and write down the order of its steps and what each one throws; then read its `catch` and note which errors keep their status.

**Visibility and ownership.** `getWorkflowVisibilityScope` decides which workflows a role can see at all, and `assertCanManageWorkflow` decides whether the actor may change a particular one. For each role, note the scope it gets. Then read `triggerWorkflowManually` in the dispatch service and list its checks in order, with the status each throws.

Finally read `allowedTransitions` in `src/lib/workflow/status-machine.ts` and draw it as a diagram of workflow statuses.

excerpts.quote: The role matrix is centralized in `src/lib/auth/permissions.ts` inside `permissionMatrix`.

readMore.why: The matrix, the visibility scope and the ownership check.
executeRoute: authentication, permission, parsing and errors.

items.title: Concept: jobs, retries, schedules and step data
items.body:
The worker loop calls `drainOnce` in `src/services/workflow-execution-service.ts`. Read it from top to bottom while you answer these from the code:

- How does `leaseNextAvailableJob` (`src/repositories/workflow-job-repository.ts`) choose a job, and which job statuses can it pick?
- In the `catch` block, how is the attempt count compared with the job's maximum, how is that maximum set when a job is created (see `workflow-run-repository.ts`), and how is the next `readyAt` computed?
- What does the scheduler's `dispatchScheduledRuns` use as the starting point when it computes the next run time?

Then read the two small helpers that feed steps their data. In `src/lib/workflow/conditions.ts`, note what `readPath` returns for a path that does not exist and how each operator converts its operands. In `src/lib/workflow/templates.ts`, note what `lookupToken` returns for a missing token. Try two or three values in a Node REPL to check yourself.

readMore.why: drainOnce: conditions, actions, success and retry paths.
How step conditions read paths and compare values.

items.title: Limit in the query, not after it
items.body:
The dashboard needs eight recent runs. It asks the repository for runs workflow by workflow, and that method has no `take`, so each call returns the workflow's entire history. The service then flattens, sorts by date in JavaScript and slices eight. For a workflow with 50,000 runs, every dashboard load pulls 50,000 rows to display a handful, and the cost grows with history instead of staying flat.

The fix is to push the limit and the ordering into SQL: one query over the visible runs with `orderBy createdAt desc` and `take 8`, served by an index on `createdAt`. The workflow list already includes the five newest runs per workflow, so even that data was available.

- *Eight* and *five* describe limits the run query does not have.
- *Two* imagines a per-workflow share.

items.title: Why a read-only analyst sees more than an operator
items.body:
`getWorkflowVisibilityScope` returns `"all"` for ADMIN and ANALYST and `"own"` for OPERATOR, and the list query filters with it. An analyst therefore sees every workflow, read-only, while an operator who created nothing sees an empty list. The auth doc calls out this asymmetry and its first exercise proves it.

- *Both see everything* is wrong: operators are scoped to their own workflows.
- *Neither sees any* is wrong for the analyst.
- *Operator all, analyst shared* reverses the two scopes, and there is no sharing model.

excerpts.quote: so an analyst sees more than an operator does.

items.title: Why a paused workflow cannot be triggered
items.body:
After the scoped load and the ownership check, `triggerWorkflowManually` compares the status with ACTIVE and throws **409 WORKFLOW_NOT_ACTIVE** "Only active workflows can be triggered manually." for anything else, PAUSED included.

- *201 when paused* is wrong: the status check applies to every manual trigger.
- *422, republish first* is wrong: 422 codes in this app are for activation readiness (steps, event name, cron), and the trigger path does not use them.
- *403, locked to admins* is wrong: the check is about status, and even admins are refused.

excerpts.quote: if (workflow.status !== WorkflowStatus.ACTIVE) { throw new AppError("Only active workflows can be triggered manually.", 409, "WORKFLOW_NOT_ACTIVE");

items.title: Concept: the builder, the dashboard and multi-row writes
items.body:
The later questions in this pack look at three things the first ones did not: the builder page in the browser, the dashboard read model, and writes that touch many rows.

**The builder.** Open `src/components/workflows/workflow-builder.tsx`. Note how server data gets into the form fields, then list each mutation and what its `onSuccess` invalidates. Read `src/hooks/use-workflow.ts` and the client defaults in `src/components/providers/app-providers.tsx` next to it.

**The dashboard.** Read `getDashboard` in `src/services/workflow-monitoring-service.ts` together with the repository methods it calls.

**Writes.** For `updateWorkflow` in the workflow repository and for `ingestEvent` in the dispatch service, mark where each transaction starts and ends. Then read the relations in `prisma/schema.prisma`.

readMore.why: How the dashboard assembles workflows, runs and stats.
Run creation and the run read queries.

items.title: Asynchronous work needs a refresh strategy in the UI
items.body:
The trigger request only enqueues: the run is created QUEUED and the worker process finishes it later. The page asks for the runs once, when the trigger mutation invalidates their key, which is before the worker has done anything. After that nothing asks again. The runs query has no `refetchInterval`, focus refetching is off, and there is no socket or server-sent event. A 30 s staleTime marks the data stale but does not fetch; it only lets the next mount fetch.

For job-style work, poll while something is in flight (`refetchInterval` that returns a number while any run is QUEUED or RUNNING and `false` otherwise), or push updates.

- *Polls every 30 seconds* confuses staleTime with an interval.
- *Pushed by the worker* needs a channel that does not exist.
- *RUNNING* is never fetched either.

items.title: Replacing child rows wholesale collides with history
items.body:
Saving a workflow never updates steps in place. `updateWorkflow` opens a transaction, deletes every step of the workflow and creates the submitted ones again. That is simple while nothing points at the steps. Once the workflow has run, each run's step-run rows reference the old step ids, and that relation is declared `onDelete: Restrict`. PostgreSQL refuses the delete, the transaction rolls back, and because the error is not an `AppError` the route answers a generic 500.

The usual fixes are an upsert-by-position that keeps step ids, or versioned definitions where runs point at an immutable snapshot. Switching the relation to `Cascade` would make the save succeed by deleting run history, which is worse.

- *History deleted* would need Cascade.
- *Updated in place* is not what the repository does.
- *409 locked* does not exist.

readMore.why: The repo's own verified finding about this edit path.

items.title: Start here: FlowForge in three processes
items.body:
FlowForge is a workflow automation engine built as a learning project. Users define workflows (a trigger plus ordered steps), and runs are executed in the background. It is three processes sharing one PostgreSQL database: the Next.js web app and REST API, a worker that polls for jobs, and a scheduler that starts cron workflows.

Read in this order:

1. `README.md`: what runs where and which environment variables matter.
2. `docs/architecture/README.md`: layers, folders and the route table.
3. `docs/architecture/request-lifecycle.md`: each request traced through files and line numbers, an error-mapping table and debugging scenarios.
4. `docs/architecture/auth-and-permissions.md` and `docs/learning/guided-reading-path.md`.

The README says plainly that nothing was run end to end against a database. Use the docs as a map and read each cited line yourself before you answer.

excerpts.quote: FlowForge is a production-style workflow automation engine built around explicit backend boundaries

readMore.why: Every main request traced, plus error mapping and debugging scenarios.
Roles, the permission matrix and visibility scope.

items.title: Why a one-character step name is a 500
items.body:
The route parses the body with the workflow schema, which requires step names of at least two characters, so `parse` throws a `ZodError`. `executeRoute`'s `catch` keeps the status only for `AppError`; every other error gets the generic **500** "An unexpected server error occurred." There is no `console.error` in that branch either, so the server leaves no trace. The lifecycle doc's error table marks this as "should be 400".

- *400 with field errors* is the fix, not today's behaviour.
- *422 WORKFLOW_STEP_REQUIRED* is the activation check for a workflow with no steps.
- *201* is wrong: the schema does validate names.

items.title: A fan-out loop of separate transactions is not atomic
items.body:
`ingestEvent` handles each matched workflow in turn, and each run is created in its own transaction. When the third creation fails, the first two runs are already committed; the error escapes the loop and the client sees a 500. Nothing marks the event as processed, so the client's retry is just a new event: all three workflows match again and the first two get a second run each.

Two standard repairs: wrap the whole fan-out in one transaction so it commits or fails as a unit, or have the caller send an event id that is stored under a unique key, so a repeat is recognised and answered from the first result. At-least-once delivery from upstream makes the second one necessary anyway.

- *One each* would need either of those repairs.
- *None* would need a rollback that spans the loop.

readMore.why: The per-run transaction each loop iteration opens.

items.title: A metric computed from a display sample
items.body:
Recent Failures is `recentRuns.filter(...).length`, and `recentRuns` is a display list: the eight newest runs drawn from the four most recently updated workflows. A workflow that has not been edited lately is outside that sample, so twenty failures today add nothing to the tile, and a burst of failures on one active workflow is capped by the eight rows anyway. The number on the card answers how many of the runs shown are failed, not how much is failing.

Operational counters should come from their own query (a count of FAILED runs in a time window, scoped like everything else), not be derived from whatever the page happens to display.

- *All 20* would need a dedicated count.
- *Five* uses the list's included runs, which the stats ignore.
- *Eight* is the list size, not a cap the stats apply.

items.title: Why a paused workflow cannot go back to draft
items.body:
`allowedTransitions` lists the moves from each status. PAUSED may go to ACTIVE or ARCHIVED only. `assertValidWorkflowTransition` returns early when the status does not change, and otherwise throws **409 INVALID_WORKFLOW_TRANSITION** for any move not in the list, which includes PAUSED to DRAFT. DRAFT is a starting state that no other status leads back to.

- *Any earlier status* is wrong: the matrix is explicit and small.
- *Only without runs* is wrong: runs are not consulted.
- *422* is wrong: DRAFT is a real status; the problem is the move, which is a 409.

items.title: Counting attempts and waits for a failing step
items.body:
When a run is created, the first job gets `maxAttempts` equal to the step's `maxRetries + 1`, so 3 here; later steps get the same formula when they are queued. In the worker's `catch`, `attempts` is the job's previous count plus one. While `attempts < maxAttempts`, the step is retried with `readyAt = now + attempts * 15 000 ms`: 15 s after the first failure, 30 s after the second. The third failure marks the step failed and the job dead.

- *Two attempts* forgets the + 1 for the original try.
- *Four attempts* counts one try too many: maxRetries 2 means three attempts in total.
- *Each after 30 s* is wrong: the wait grows linearly with the attempt number.

items.title: What a missing template token turns into
items.body:
`resolveTemplateStrings` replaces each `{{...}}` with `String(lookupToken(context, token))`. `lookupToken` walks the dotted path and returns an empty string as soon as a segment is missing. So `{{payload.orderId}}` becomes `""` and the request goes to `https://api.test/orders/`. The testing rationale records this as checked behaviour, along with `"[object Object]"` for an object token.

- *Placeholder kept* is wrong: every match of the pattern is replaced.
- *"undefined" in the URL* is wrong: the lookup returns `""`, not `undefined`.
- *A missing-variable error* is wrong: nothing throws for a missing token.

items.title: One entry point checks scope, the other does not
items.body:
Running a workflow by hand goes through a scoped read: an operator who cannot see a workflow gets 404. Running it by event does not. The ingest route needs only `workflow:execute`, and `listActiveEventWorkflows` takes nothing but the event name, so it returns every matching event workflow in the system, whoever owns it. Operator A's event therefore starts B's workflow, and the run is recorded as initiated by A.

Whether that is a bug depends on the product: a shared event bus may be intended. If it is not, the repository method needs the caller's scope, exactly like the manual path, so that authorization lives in the query rather than in each caller.

- *Only the caller's workflows* describes a filter that is not there.
- *404 like a manual run* applies to the manual path only.
- *Only for admins or analysts* mixes in the read scope.

items.title: Why a scheduled workflow can also be run by hand
items.body:
The manual trigger checks visibility, ownership and that the workflow is ACTIVE. It never looks at `triggerType`, so a SCHEDULE workflow is accepted like any other. It re-reads the workflow with its ordered steps and enqueues a run with the source `"manual"`, answered with **201**. `nextScheduledAt` is advanced only by the scheduler's dispatch, not here.

- *409, cron only* would need a trigger-type check, which does not exist.
- *422, needs an event name* is an activation rule for EVENT workflows, not a trigger rule.
- *nextScheduledAt moves ahead* is wrong: the manual path does not touch it.

items.title: Why a job leased by a dead worker never comes back
items.body:
`leaseNextAvailableJob` picks one row with `status = 'AVAILABLE'` whose `readyAt` has passed, and sets it to LEASED with a token and a 30-second `leasedUntil`. No code ever turns an expired LEASED row back into AVAILABLE, and the lease query does not consider LEASED rows at all. If the worker dies, the job stays LEASED and the run stays RUNNING. The lifecycle doc's debugging scenario 4 describes this and the fix.

- *Re-leased after 30 s* is how it should work; `leasedUntil` is written but not used to reclaim.
- *Reset by the scheduler* is wrong: the scheduler only dispatches due cron workflows.
- *Marked dead* is wrong: `markDead` runs only after a final failure inside a live worker.
